92286.q: What part of the carrot grows above the ground?
92286.e: Above the ground you only see the green tops with finely feathered leaves. The orange root is in the soil.
92286.m: Carrot tops have finely feathered leaves.

92287.q: Carrots are good for one part of our body. Which one?
92287.e: Carrots contain a substance that the body turns into vitamin A. Our eyes need it to see.
92287.m: Carrots are good for your eyes.

92288.q: When does a carrot flower if you leave it in the ground?
92288.e: The carrot is a biennial. In the first year the root grows, and in the second year it flowers and makes seeds.
92288.m: The carrot only flowers in its second year.

92291.q: What is traditionally eaten with melted raclette cheese?
92291.e: Raclette comes with potatoes boiled in their skins. There are often pickled gherkins and silverskin onions too.

92292.q: Can you eat the small green berries of the potato plant?
92292.e: After flowering, small green berries form. They contain poison and must not be eaten.
92292.m: The berries of the potato plant are poisonous.

92293.q: What colour are potato flowers often?
92293.e: Potatoes flower in summer. Depending on the variety, the flowers are white, pink or purple.
92293.m: Potatoes have white or purple flowers.

92294.q: Where is the best place to store potatoes?
92294.e: Potatoes are stored in a cool, dark place, for example in the cellar. That way they sprout less quickly.
92294.m: Store potatoes somewhere cool and dark.

92295.q: Which potato dish is cut into strips and deep-fried?
92295.e: For chips, you cut potatoes into strips. Then they are deep-fried in hot oil.
92295.m: Chips are deep-fried strips of potato.

92297.e: Young tomatoes are green at first. Only when they ripen do most of them turn red.

92298.q: Which tomato sauce do people often eat with chips?
92298.e: Ketchup is made mainly from tomatoes, sugar and vinegar. Lots of people eat it with chips.

92299.q: Which continent does the tomato originally come from?
92299.e: The tomato comes from Central and South America. Sailors brought it to Europe about 500 years ago.
92299.m: The tomato originally comes from America.

92300.e: Tomato plants have small yellow flowers. The tomatoes later grow from them.

92301.q: When are tomatoes usually planted outdoors in Switzerland?
92301.e: Tomatoes cannot cope with frost. That is why they are only planted outdoors after the “Ice Saints” in mid-May.
92301.m: Tomatoes are only planted outdoors after mid-May.

92302.q: What is usually spread on a pizza base first?
92302.e: Most pizzas get tomato sauce first. Then come cheese and other toppings.
92302.m: Tomato sauce goes on the pizza first.

92303.q: What are tomato plants in the garden often tied to?
92303.e: Tomato plants grow tall and the fruits are heavy. A cane supports the plant so that it does not snap.
92303.m: Tomatoes are tied to a cane.

92304.q: What are small, round tomatoes that you can easily eat whole called?
92304.e: Cherry tomatoes are as small as cherries, which is where they get their name.
92304.m: Cherry tomatoes are as small as cherries.

92305.q: Which part of a lettuce do we eat?
92305.e: With lettuce, you eat the tender leaves. The root stays in the ground.
92305.m: We eat the leaves of lettuce.

92306.q: Why is it called head lettuce?
a: Its leaves form a round head
It is as hard as a head
92306.e: The leaves grow tightly on top of each other and form a round shape. This shape is called a head.
92306.m: Head lettuce forms a round head of leaves.

92307.q: Which animals in the garden especially like to eat lettuce?
92307.e: Slugs and snails love tender lettuce leaves. They often eat at night and in damp weather.
92307.m: Slugs and snails like eating lettuce leaves.

92308.e: Lettuce is usually eaten raw as a salad. You wash the leaves well first.

92309.q: What do you add to lettuce to make it taste better?
92309.e: You mix the salad with a dressing made of oil, vinegar and seasoning. That makes it taste nicer.

92310.q: What happens to lettuce when it is hot for a long time?
a: It becomes as hard as wood
92310.e: In hot weather, lettuce grows a tall stem with flowers. This is called bolting, and the leaves become bitter.
92310.m: In hot weather lettuce shoots up.

92311.q: What colour are lettuce leaves usually?
92311.e: Most lettuces have green leaves. There are also varieties with reddish leaves.

92312.q: What is a young lettuce plant that you plant in the garden called?
92312.e: A small, young plant for planting out is called a seedling. Lettuce is often planted this way.
92312.m: A young plant for planting out is called a seedling.

92313.q: Which meadow flower is lettuce related to?
92313.e: Lettuce and dandelions both belong to the daisy family. Both have a white milky sap.
92313.m: Lettuce is related to the dandelion.

92314.q: What colour is the skin of a cucumber?
92314.e: The skin of the cucumber is green. Inside, the flesh is pale.
92314.m: The cucumber has a green skin.

92315.e: Cucumber plants have yellow flowers. The cucumbers grow from some of the flowers.

92316.q: What are small cucumbers pickled in vinegar called?
92316.e: Small cucumbers are pickled in vinegar with spices. That way they keep for a long time and are called cornichons.

92317.q: Which plant is the cucumber related to?
92317.e: Cucumbers and pumpkins are close relatives. Both have yellow flowers and grow on long vines.
92317.m: The cucumber is related to the pumpkin.

92318.q: What is a cucumber mostly made of?
92318.e: A cucumber is made almost entirely of water. That is why it is so juicy and refreshing.
92318.m: A cucumber is almost all water.

92319.q: How is a cucumber usually cut for cucumber salad?
92319.e: For cucumber salad, you cut or slice the cucumber thinly. That way it soaks up the dressing well.
92319.m: For cucumber salad you cut thin slices.

92320.q: What do you find inside a cucumber?
92320.e: In the middle of the cucumber there are lots of small, soft seeds. They are the seeds of the plant.
92320.m: A cucumber contains lots of small seeds.

92321.q: Where do cucumbers often grow in Switzerland so that they are warm enough?
92321.e: Cucumbers like it warm and humid. That is why many cucumbers grow in greenhouses.

92323.e: Most courgettes are dark green. There are also yellow varieties.

92324.q: Apart from the fruit, which part of the courgette plant can you eat?
92324.e: You can eat the big yellow flowers of the courgette. For example, people stuff them or fry them in batter.
92324.m: You can also eat courgette flowers.

92325.q: How does a courgette plant usually grow?
a: As a big bush with huge leaves
As a tall tree with branches
As a tuber under the ground
As a water plant in a pond
92325.e: The courgette plant usually grows like a bush and has very large leaves. The fruits grow low down on the thick stem.
92325.m: The courgette grows as a big bush.

92326.q: What does the Italian word “zucchini” mean?
92326.e: In Italian, the pumpkin or squash is called “zucca”. So zucchini means little pumpkins. In Britain they are called courgettes.

92327.q: What happens to a courgette that is not picked in time?
92327.e: Courgettes keep growing very quickly. If they are left on the plant, they become huge and their skin gets hard.

92328.q: Why does a family often need only a few courgette plants?
a: Each plant produces lots of fruits
They only grow every ten years
92328.e: A single courgette plant produces lots of fruits in summer. That is why a few plants are enough for a family.
92328.m: A courgette plant produces lots of fruits.

92329.q: What is the name of a vegetable dish from France with courgettes, tomatoes and peppers?
92329.e: Ratatouille comes from the south of France. Courgettes, tomatoes, peppers and aubergines are stewed in it.
92329.m: Ratatouille is a vegetable dish with courgettes.

92330.q: At which autumn festival do people carve faces into pumpkins?
92330.e: At Halloween at the end of October, people hollow out pumpkins and carve faces into them. A candle shines inside.
92330.m: At Halloween people carve pumpkin faces.

92331.q: Apart from the flesh, what else can you eat from a pumpkin?
92331.e: You can roast and eat pumpkin seeds. They are also pressed to make oil.

92332.q: How heavy can the biggest giant pumpkins at competitions get?
92332.e: The heaviest pumpkins in the world weigh more than a tonne. That is heavier than a small car.
92332.m: Giant pumpkins can weigh over a tonne.

92333.q: In which season are pumpkins harvested?
92333.e: Pumpkins grow all summer. In autumn they are ripe and are harvested.

92334.q: What colour is the Hokkaido pumpkin usually?
92334.e: The Hokkaido pumpkin is usually bright orange. You can cook and eat its skin too.

92335.q: What is a pumpkin actually, according to plant scientists?
92335.e: The pumpkin is a fruit with seeds inside. Because its rind is hard, it is called an armoured berry (a pepo).
92335.m: The pumpkin is a berry with a hard rind.

92336.q: Why should you not eat ornamental gourds?
92336.e: Ornamental gourds often contain bitter substances that are poisonous. They are only for decoration.
92336.m: Do not eat ornamental gourds, as they can be poisonous.

92337.q: How long can many whole pumpkins be stored somewhere cool and dry?
92337.e: The hard rind protects the pumpkin. That is why it can often be stored for months somewhere cool and dry.
92337.m: A whole pumpkin often keeps for several months.

92338.q: What is the case that peas grow in called?
92338.e: Peas grow in a long green pod. It is also called a shell.

92339.q: What colour are fresh peas usually?
92339.e: Fresh peas are green and slightly sweet. Dried peas can also be yellow.

92341.q: Which scientist did famous experiments on inheritance using peas?
92341.e: Gregor Mendel crossed lots of peas in his monastery garden. This is how he found rules for how characteristics are passed on.
92341.m: Gregor Mendel did research with peas.

92342.q: In which fairy tale is there a pea under lots of mattresses?
92342.e: In the fairy tale by Hans Christian Andersen, a real princess feels the little pea through lots of mattresses.
92342.m: The princess feels the pea through lots of mattresses.

92343.e: Peas are small round balls. They can easily roll away.

92344.q: How do fresh peas stay green for a long time after harvest?
a: They are put in the sun
They are put in warm water
They are left lying open in a room
92344.e: Peas are frozen quickly after harvest. This keeps them fresh and green for a long time.
92344.m: Frozen peas stay fresh for a long time.

92345.q: What is a pea actually, for the plant?
92345.e: The pea is the seed of the pea plant. If you put it in the soil, a new plant grows.

92346.q: Why must you not eat green beans raw?
a: They are too hard to bite
92346.e: Raw beans contain a poisonous substance. Cooking destroys it.

92347.q: What is the bean called that climbs up long poles?
92347.e: The climbing bean grows very tall. That is why long poles are pushed into the ground for it to climb up.
92347.m: The climbing bean climbs up poles.

92348.q: What is the bean called that grows low and does not need a pole?
92348.e: The dwarf bean grows as a small bush. It does not need anything to climb up.
92348.m: The dwarf bean grows low like a bush.

92349.q: What is the red bean that is often in chilli con carne called?
92349.e: The kidney bean is a red variety of the common bean. It gets its name from its kidney shape.
92349.m: The kidney bean is red and shaped like a kidney.

92350.q: How does the climbing bean climb upwards?
a: Its stem winds around the pole
92350.e: The climbing bean has no tendrils. Its whole stem winds round and round the pole.
92350.m: The bean winds its stem around the pole.

92351.e: Wax beans are yellow green beans. Their colour is like wax.
92351.m: Yellow beans are called wax beans.

92352.q: What are the dried green beans that people in Switzerland eat with the Bernese platter called?
92352.e: In the past, beans were dried so they could be eaten in winter. These dried beans are still part of the Bernese platter today.
92352.m: Dried beans are part of the Bernese platter.

92353.q: Which part of the plant do you eat with green beans?
a: The whole pod with the seeds
92353.e: With green beans you eat the young, tender pod together with the little seeds inside. You must cook them first.
92353.m: With green beans you eat the whole pod.

92354.q: What colour is a radish on the outside, usually?
92354.e: Most radishes are bright red on the outside. There are also white varieties.
92354.m: Radishes are usually red on the outside.

92355.q: What colour is a radish on the inside?
92355.e: Inside, the radish is white. Only the thin skin is red.

92356.e: Radishes contain hot substances that taste a bit like mustard. That is why they burn a little on your tongue.

92357.q: Roughly how long does it take from sowing to harvesting radishes?
92357.e: Radishes grow very quickly. You can harvest them just a few weeks after sowing.
92357.m: Radishes grow in a few weeks.

92358.q: What shape is a typical radish?
92358.e: The typical radish is small and round. But there are also longer varieties.

92359.q: Which bigger, white vegetable is the radish closely related to?
92359.e: The small red radish and the large white radish belong to the same plant species. Both taste peppery.
92359.m: The radish is related to the white radish.

92360.q: What happens to radishes that stay in the ground too long?
92360.e: If radishes stay in the soil too long, they go woody or spongy inside. Then they no longer taste good.

a: Yes, for example in a salad
92361.e: Radish leaves are edible. You can put them in salad, soup or pesto.
92361.m: You can eat radish leaves too.

a: White at the bottom, green at the top
Red at the bottom, yellow at the top
Black at the bottom, white at the top
92362.e: The lower part of the leek is white because it grows in the ground. At the top the leaves are green.
92362.m: Leeks are white at the bottom and green at the top.

92363.q: Which vegetable is the leek related to?
92363.e: Leeks and onions belong to the same plant genus. Both smell and taste similar.
92363.m: The leek is related to the onion.

92364.q: Which dish from the canton of Vaud is made with leeks and potatoes?
92364.e: Papet vaudois is a stew of leeks and potatoes. It is eaten with a Vaud sausage.

92365.q: Can you harvest leeks in the garden in winter too?
a: Yes, they can cope with cold
No, they freeze to death straight away
92365.e: Winter varieties of leek can cope with frost. So you can harvest them in winter too.
92365.m: You can harvest leeks in winter too.

92366.q: What do you do to make the white part of the leek longer?
92366.e: You pile soil up around the leek. Whatever grows in the dark stays white.
92366.m: Piling up soil keeps more of the leek white.

92367.q: Which country has the leek as its symbol?
92367.e: The leek is a national symbol of Wales. Scotland has the thistle and Ireland the shamrock.
92367.m: The leek is a symbol of Wales.

92368.q: Where is there often soil in a leek that you have to wash out?
a: In the middle of a stone
92368.e: As the leek grows, soil trickles between the leaves. That is why you cut the leek open and wash it well.
92368.m: Wash leeks well between the leaves.

92370.q: Why do your eyes water when you cut onions?
a: A substance from the onion irritates your eyes
92370.e: When you cut it, a sharp substance is released and rises into the air. It irritates your eyes and they water.
92370.m: A substance from the onion makes your eyes water.

92371.q: What is the famous onion market in Bern called?
92371.e: At the Zibelemärit, farmers sell lots of onions in Bern's old town. It is a big public festival.

92372.q: In which month does the Zibelemärit in Bern take place?
92372.e: The Zibelemärit is held every year in November. Then Bern's old town is full of market stalls with onions.

92373.q: What is plaited from onions and sold at the Zibelemärit?
92373.e: At the Zibelemärit you can buy beautifully plaited strings of onions. You can hang them up and store them for a long time.

92374.q: What colour is the dry skin of most cooking onions?
92374.e: Most onions have a golden brown, paper-thin skin. There are also red and white onions.
92374.m: Most onions have a golden brown skin.

92375.q: What does an onion taste like when you cook it slowly in the pan for a long time?
92375.e: When cooked slowly, the onion loses its sharpness. It goes soft and tastes sweet.

92376.q: Which kitchen herb is related to the onion?
92376.e: Chives and onions belong to the same plant genus. Chives have thin, hollow, tube-shaped leaves.
92376.m: Chives are related to the onion.

92377.q: What are the small onions that you put into the garden soil in spring called?
92377.e: Onion sets are small onions. You push them into the soil and they grow into big onions.
92377.m: Onion sets are pushed into the soil.

92378.q: What grows out of an onion that has been lying in the kitchen for a long time?
92378.e: An old onion starts to sprout. Green shoots grow out of the top.

92476.q: Which animal has horizontal, oblong pupils?
92476.e: Goats and sheep have oblong pupils that lie sideways. That way they can see a lot of their surroundings while grazing.

92477.q: What happens to the pupil in bright light?
92477.e: In bright light the pupil narrows. That way not too much light gets into the eye.
92477.m: In bright light the pupil gets small.

92478.q: What happens to the pupil in the dark?
92478.e: In the dark the pupil opens wide. That way more light can get into the eye.
92478.m: In the dark the pupil gets big.

a: It lets light into the eye
92479.e: The pupil is the window of the eye. Light can only get inside through it.
92479.m: Light enters the eye through the pupil.

92480.q: Why does the pupil look black?
a: Hardly any light comes back out of it
92480.e: Light passes through the pupil into the dark inside of the eye. Almost nothing comes back out, so it looks black.
92480.m: The pupil looks black because almost no light comes back out of the eye.

92481.q: What shape is the human pupil?
92481.e: In humans the pupil is a round circle. Some animals have other shapes.

92482.q: Which animal often has a narrow, slit-shaped pupil during the day?
92482.e: In cats the pupil becomes a narrow slit in bright light. In the dark it becomes almost completely round.
92482.m: Cats have slit-shaped pupils in bright light.

92483.q: Why do eyes sometimes look red in photos taken with a flash?
a: The flash hits the blood vessels in the eye
92483.e: The flash shines through the pupil onto the back of the eye, which has lots of blood vessels. The red light comes back into the camera.
92483.m: Red eyes in photos come from the flash.

92484.q: What is the coloured ring around the pupil called?
92484.e: The iris is the coloured part of the eye. It lies all around the pupil.
92484.m: The iris is the coloured ring in the eye.

a: It makes the pupil bigger or smaller
92486.e: The iris has tiny muscles. They change the size of the pupil like the aperture of a camera.
92486.m: The iris controls how much light gets into the eye.

92487.q: What does the Greek word “iris” mean?
92487.e: Iris is the Greek word for rainbow. In Greek myths, a messenger of the gods was also called Iris.

92488.q: What can the pattern of the iris be used for?
92488.e: The pattern of the iris is different in every person. That is why machines can recognise a person by their iris.
92488.m: Every person has their own iris pattern.

92489.q: Which see-through layer lies in front of the iris?
92489.e: The cornea is as clear as the glass on a watch. It protects the iris and helps us see sharply.
92489.m: The see-through cornea lies in front of the iris.

92490.q: What is the white of the eye called?
92490.e: The sclera is the tough, white outer layer of the eye. It surrounds the coloured iris.
92490.m: The white of the eye is the sclera.

92491.q: Which eye colour is the most common in the world?
92491.e: Most people on Earth have brown eyes. Blue and green eyes are much rarer.
92491.m: Brown is the most common eye colour in the world.

92492.q: Which of these eye colours is the rarest?
92492.e: Only a few people in the world have green eyes. Brown eyes are the most common.

92493.q: In which part of the world do especially many people have blue eyes?
92493.e: Blue eyes are fairly rare worldwide. But in countries like Sweden or Finland, a great many people have blue eyes.
92493.m: Many people in northern Europe have blue eyes.

92494.q: Who do you get your eye colour from?
92494.e: Eye colour is inherited. It depends on the genes from your mother and father.
92494.m: You inherit your eye colour from your parents.

92495.q: Can a person have two different eye colours?
92495.e: Some people have, for example, one blue eye and one brown eye. This is rare and usually harmless.
92495.m: Two different eye colours are rare.

92496.q: Is there a blue pigment in blue eyes?
a: No, the blue comes from scattered light
Yes, a blue pigment in the iris
Yes, a blue pigment from the blood
Yes, a blue pigment in the tears
92496.e: Blue eyes have only a little pigment. The blue appears because light is scattered in the iris, a bit like with the sky.
92496.m: Blue eyes have no blue pigment.

92497.q: What eye colour do many fair-skinned babies have at birth?
92497.e: At birth, many fair-skinned babies still have little pigment in the iris. That is why their eyes are often blue or grey.
92497.m: Many babies have blue or grey eyes at first.

92498.q: When can a child's eye colour still change?
a: In the first years of life
92498.e: The pigment in the iris keeps forming after birth. That is why eye colour can still get darker in the first years of life.
92498.m: Small children's eye colour can still change.

92499.q: What do the eyes of people with albinism often look like?
92499.e: People with albinism have very little pigment in their bodies. That is why their eyes are often light blue or have a reddish shimmer.
92499.m: With albinism the eyes are often very pale.

92500.q: What are tears mostly made of?
92500.e: Tears are almost entirely water. There are also small amounts of salt and other substances.

92501.e: The tear gland lies above the eye. It constantly makes tear fluid.
92501.m: Tears come from the tear gland.

a: Above the eye, towards the outside
92502.e: The tear gland sits at the top outer edge of the eye socket. From there the fluid flows over the eye.
92502.m: The tear gland is at the top outer side of the eye.

92503.q: What are tears good for, even when you are not crying?
92503.e: A thin film of tears always covers the eye. It keeps it moist and washes away tiny bits of dust.
92503.m: Tears keep the eye moist and clean.

92504.q: What can help with dry eyes?
92504.e: Artificial tears come as eye drops. They moisten the eye when there are not enough natural tears.
92504.m: Artificial tears help with dry eyes.

92505.q: Why does your nose often run when you cry?
92505.e: A small duct leads from the inner corner of the eye into the nose. When you cry, a lot of tear fluid flows into it.
92505.m: Tears flow through a duct into the nose.

92506.q: What do tears do to germs in the eye?
92506.e: Tear fluid contains substances that harm bacteria. That way tears protect the eye from infections.
92506.m: Tears protect the eye from germs.

92507.q: What is different when many newborn babies cry?
92507.e: In the first weeks babies often make few tears. That is why they often cry without wet eyes.
92507.m: Newborn babies often cry without tears.

92508.q: Roughly how many times a minute does a person blink?
92508.e: A blink only lasts a fraction of a second. We usually blink without noticing.
92508.m: We blink several times a minute without noticing.

92509.q: Why do people wear glasses with specially shaped lenses?
92509.e: Glasses bend the light so that a sharp image forms on the retina. That way you can see clearly again.

92510.q: What is the job called in which you fit and sell glasses?
92510.e: Opticians measure the eyes and make the right lenses. They fit the glasses to the face.
92510.m: You get glasses from an optician.

92511.q: What can you put directly on your eye instead of glasses?
92511.e: Contact lenses are small, thin shells. They sit directly on the cornea and work like the lenses in glasses.
92511.m: Contact lenses sit directly on the eye.

a: You can only see in the dark
92512.e: Short-sighted people see things close up sharply, but things far away look blurred. Glasses can correct this.
92512.m: Short-sighted people see things far away blurred.

92513.e: Long-sighted people find it hard to see things close up sharply. They often see things far away better.
92513.m: Long-sighted people see badly close up.

92514.q: Why do many older people need reading glasses?
a: The lens of the eye gets stiffer
92514.e: With age the lens in the eye can no longer change shape so well. That is why many people over about 45 see blurred close up.
92514.m: Many people need reading glasses as they get older.

92515.q: What happens to glasses in winter when you come into a warm house?
92515.e: The cold lenses cool down the warm, moist air. Tiny water droplets form on the glass.
92515.m: Cold lenses steam up in warm air.

92516.q: What is the part of the glasses that rests on the nose called?
92516.e: The bridge joins the two lenses. It rests on the top of the nose and carries the weight of the glasses.
92516.m: The bridge of the glasses rests on the nose.

92517.q: What does an eye test check?
92517.e: An eye test measures how sharply someone sees. That shows whether glasses are needed.
92517.m: An eye test checks how well your eyes see.

92518.q: What do you often read on the wall during an eye test?
a: Symbols that get smaller and smaller
92518.e: The eye chart has symbols of different sizes. The smaller the symbols you can make out, the better you see.
92518.m: On the eye chart the symbols get smaller and smaller.

92519.q: Why do you cover one eye during an eye test?
a: Because those are the rules of the game
92519.e: Often one eye sees better than the other. That is why each eye is tested on its own.
92519.m: In an eye test each eye is tested separately.

92520.q: What do you have to say in an eye test with rings?
92520.e: In the eye test with Landolt rings, each ring has a small gap. You say whether it is at the top, bottom, left or right.
92520.m: In the ring test you show where the gap is.

92521.q: What are small children shown in an eye test instead of letters?
92521.e: Children who cannot read yet name pictures or show which way symbols point. That way their eyes can be tested too.
92521.m: Small children do the eye test with pictures.

92522.q: For which licence do you need an eye test in Switzerland?
92522.e: Anyone in Switzerland who wants to learn to drive has to take an eye test. Only then do they get a learner driver's permit.
92522.m: You need an eye test to drive a car.

92523.q: What do we call how sharply someone sees?
92523.e: Visual acuity tells you how finely someone can make things out. It is measured in an eye test.
92523.m: An eye test measures visual acuity.

92524.q: Where can you have a simple eye test done?
92524.e: Opticians and eye doctors do eye tests. For detailed examinations you go to an eye doctor.
92524.m: You have an eye test at the optician's or the eye doctor's.

92525.q: What is the doctor who examines and treats eyes called?
92525.e: Eye doctors know all about diseases of the eyes. They can also operate on eyes.
92525.m: For eye problems you go to an eye doctor.

92526.q: Why does the eye doctor sometimes put drops in your eye?
92526.e: With a wide pupil the doctor can see better inside the eye. Afterwards your vision is a little blurry for a few hours.
92526.m: Special drops widen the pupil for the examination.

92527.q: What do you read on a chart on the wall at the eye doctor's?
a: Letters that get smaller and smaller
92527.e: The eye chart has letters or pictures that get smaller and smaller towards the bottom. That shows the doctor how well you see.
92527.m: The eye doctor uses the eye chart to check how well I see.

92528.q: What is a common inflammation called in which the eye turns red and itches?
92528.e: The conjunctiva covers the white of the eye and the inside of the eyelids. When it is inflamed, the eye turns red and itches.
92528.m: With conjunctivitis the eye is red.

92529.q: What is a small, inflamed lump on the eyelid called?
92529.e: A stye is an infection of a small gland at the edge of the eyelid. It is red and sore and usually heals by itself.
92529.m: A stye is an inflammation on the eyelid.

92530.q: What is replaced in an operation for cataracts?
92530.e: With cataracts, the lens in the eye becomes cloudy. In the operation an artificial, clear lens is put in.
92530.m: With cataracts the cloudy lens is replaced.

92531.q: What should you do if something sharp has got into your eye?
a: Don't rub it and go to a doctor
92531.e: Rubbing can injure the eye even more. That is why you go to a doctor or to A&E straight away.
92531.m: With an eye injury, go to a doctor straight away.

92532.q: What does the eye doctor often give you for an eye infection?
a: A plaster cast on your leg
92532.e: Many eye infections are treated with drops or ointment. They are put straight into the eye.
92532.m: Eye infections are often treated with drops.

92533.q: What does having a squint mean?
a: The eyes look in different directions
92533.e: With a squint, the two eyes don't point at the same target. One eye turns inwards, outwards, up or down.
92533.m: With a squint, the eyes don't look in the same direction.

92534.q: What do children with a squint often have stuck over one eye?
92534.e: A special patch covers one eye for a few hours a day. This is a common treatment for a squint.
92534.m: An eye patch helps many children with a squint.

92535.q: Why is the better eye covered when someone has a squint?
a: So the weaker eye gets trained
92535.e: When the good eye is covered, the weaker eye has to work. That way it learns to see better.
92535.m: Covering the good eye trains the weaker eye.

92536.q: Why should a squint in children be treated early?
a: Otherwise one eye learns to see badly
Otherwise the eyes water all the time
92536.e: The brain can ignore the image from the squinting eye. If it is not treated early, this eye stays weak-sighted.
92536.m: A squint is best treated early.

92537.q: What can often help with a squint as well?
92537.e: Some children squint because they are long-sighted. The right glasses can then reduce the squint.
92537.m: Glasses can help with a squint.

92538.q: When is a slight squint still normal in babies?
a: In the first months of life
92538.e: Newborn babies first have to learn to use their eyes together. If the squint lasts longer, an eye doctor should take a look.
92538.m: A brief squint is normal in young babies.

92539.q: What does someone often see if they suddenly start to squint?
92539.e: The two eyes then send two different images. The brain can no longer put them together.
92539.m: A sudden squint can cause double vision.

92540.q: How many muscles move an eye from the outside?
92540.e: Six outer eye muscles pull on each eye. They work together so that both eyes look in the same direction.

92541.q: What is sometimes done for a very strong squint?
a: An operation on the eye muscles
92541.e: In the operation, eye muscles are shortened or moved. Afterwards the eyes are straighter.
92541.m: A strong squint can be operated on.

92542.q: What do good sunglasses protect the eyes from?
92542.e: Good sunglasses keep out the dangerous UV rays. They also soften dazzling light.

92543.q: Where are sunglasses especially important in Switzerland?
a: In the snow in the mountains
92543.e: UV radiation is stronger in the mountains. The snow also reflects a lot of light back into the eyes.
92543.m: You need sunglasses in the snow in the mountains.

92544.q: What can happen in the snow without sunglasses?
92544.e: Too much UV light can burn the cornea. The eyes then hurt badly and you can't see well for a while.
92544.m: Without sunglasses you risk snow blindness.

92545.q: Can you look straight at the sun with sunglasses on?
a: Yes, for as long as you like
92545.e: Even sunglasses don't protect enough against direct sunlight. The eye can be permanently damaged.
92545.m: Never look straight at the sun.

92546.q: What do you need to watch a solar eclipse?
92546.e: Eclipse glasses only let through a tiny part of the light. Ordinary sunglasses are far too bright for this.
92546.m: Only watch a solar eclipse with special glasses.

92547.q: Why are dark glasses without UV protection bad?
a: The pupil gets big and more UV gets in
92547.e: Behind dark lenses the pupil opens. If there is no UV filter, even more harmful radiation then gets into the eye.
92547.m: Sunglasses always need a UV filter.

92548.q: What do people often wear when skiing instead of sunglasses?
92548.e: Ski goggles fit tightly against the face. They protect against sun, wind and snow.
92548.m: People often wear ski goggles when skiing.

92549.q: On which surfaces does the sun reflect especially strongly?
a: On soil and sand in the shade
92549.e: Snow and water reflect a lot of sunlight. The light then also hits the eyes from below.
92549.m: Snow and water reflect sunlight strongly.

92550.q: What helps blind people read texts on a computer?
92550.e: A screen reader reads out the texts on the screen with a computer voice. Some devices also show the text in Braille on a strip you can feel.
92550.m: Screen readers read texts aloud to blind people.

92551.q: Who invented the dot writing system for blind people?
92551.e: He went blind as a small boy. At the age of 15 he developed a writing system made of dots, which is named after him.
92551.m: The dot writing for blind people is named Braille after its inventor.

92552.q: What is the largest number of dots that one Braille character has?
92552.e: A Braille character has six dots in two columns. Depending on which dots are raised, a different letter is formed.
92552.m: A Braille character has up to six dots.

92553.q: Which country did the inventor of the dot writing for blind people come from?
92553.e: The inventor was born in France in 1809. He lived and taught in Paris.
92553.m: The inventor of Braille came from France.

92554.q: What colour is the cane that blind people use?
92554.e: The white cane shows other people that someone is blind. It is used to feel the way ahead.
92554.m: Blind people use a white cane.

92555.q: What helps blind people find their way on the pavement?
92555.e: In Switzerland there are white guide lines with grooves on the ground. You can feel them with a cane or your feet.
92555.m: White guide lines with grooves lead blind people.

92556.q: Which senses help blind people find their way especially well?
92556.e: Blind people pay close attention to sounds and feel their surroundings. That way they make up for part of their missing sight.
92556.m: Blind people find their way using hearing and touch.

92557.q: Where do you often find Braille in everyday life?
92557.e: Many medicine packets have the name in Braille. That way blind people can tell them apart.

92558.q: What is a guide dog for the blind?
a: A dog that leads blind people safely
A dog that searches for avalanche victims
92558.e: A guide dog is specially trained. It leads its person safely around obstacles.
92558.m: A guide dog leads blind people.

92559.q: Which dog breed is often trained as a guide dog?
92559.e: Labradors are calm, friendly and like to learn. That is why they are often trained as guide dogs.

92560.q: What does a guide dog wear when it is working?
92560.e: The guide harness has a firm handle. Through it the person feels every movement of the dog.
92560.m: A guide dog wears a harness.

92561.q: Should you stroke a guide dog while it is working?
a: Yes, but only on the head
92561.e: A working guide dog has to concentrate fully on the way. Distracting it can be dangerous for its person.

92562.q: What does a guide dog do when something is in the way?
a: It leads its person around it
92562.e: A guide dog learns to recognise obstacles. It leads its person safely past them.
92562.m: A guide dog leads around obstacles.

92563.q: Where does a young guide dog live before it is trained?
92563.e: With the puppy-raising family, the young dog gets to know everyday life. After that the real training begins.
92563.m: Young guide dogs grow up with a puppy-raising family.

92564.q: Who decides when to cross the road?
92564.e: The person listens to the traffic and gives the command. The dog then leads them safely across.
92564.m: The person decides when to cross the road.

92565.q: What does a guide dog do in front of stairs?
92565.e: The dog stops in front of stairs and kerbs. That way its person knows a step is coming.
92565.m: A guide dog stops in front of stairs.

92566.q: What do most people who are called colour-blind have?
a: They can only see at night
92566.e: Only very few people are completely colour-blind. Most of them just find it hard to tell certain colours apart.
92566.m: Most colour-blind people only mix up some colours.

92567.q: Which colours are most often mixed up by people with colour vision deficiency?
92567.e: The most common form is red-green colour blindness. People with it see red and green as similar.
92567.m: Red and green are the colours most often mixed up.

92568.q: Who more often has red-green colour blindness?
92568.e: It is inherited in a way that makes it much more common in men. Women are only rarely affected.
92568.m: Men more often have red-green colour blindness.

92569.q: Roughly how many out of 100 men in Europe have red-green colour blindness?
92569.e: In Europe about 8 to 9 out of 100 men are affected. In women it is fewer than 1 in 100.
92569.m: About one man in twelve has red-green colour blindness.

92570.q: How do you test whether someone sees colours well?
a: With pictures made of coloured dots
92570.e: A number made of coloured dots is hidden in the test pictures. People who mix up certain colours cannot see it.
92570.m: A colour test shows numbers made of coloured dots.

92571.q: Where does red-green colour blindness usually come from?
92571.e: Red-green colour blindness is usually inherited. It is not catching and lasts a lifetime.
92571.m: Red-green colour blindness is usually present from birth.

92572.q: What are the sensory cells in the eye that see colours called?
92572.e: The retina has three kinds of these cells for different colours. If one kind is missing, you see colours differently.
92572.m: The cones in the eye see colours.

92573.q: How do colour-blind people know which traffic light is on?
a: By the position of the light
By the sound of the cars
92573.e: The order of the lights on traffic lights is always the same. Red is at the top, green is at the bottom.
92573.m: At traffic lights, the position of the light helps.

92574.q: Why do we see almost no colours at night?
a: The colour cells need a lot of light
92574.e: In the dark, mainly sensory cells that only tell light from dark are working. That is why everything looks grey at night.
92574.m: All cats are grey in the dark, because we can hardly see colours.

92575.q: Why does a banana look yellow?
92575.e: Light contains many colours. The banana skin swallows most of them and mainly reflects yellow back into our eyes.
92575.m: We see the colour that a thing reflects.

92576.q: Which colour reflects almost all light?
92576.e: White things hardly swallow any light. That is why fresh snow is so dazzling in the sun.

92577.q: Which colour swallows almost all light?
92577.e: Black things hardly reflect any light. The swallowed light turns into heat.

92578.q: Why are the leaves of trees green in summer?
a: The green pigment reflects green light
92578.e: Leaves contain a pigment called chlorophyll. It uses red and blue light and reflects the green.
92578.m: Leaves are green because they reflect green light.

92579.q: What is needed for us to see colours?
92579.e: Colours only appear when light falls on things. Without light we can't see any colours.
92579.m: Without light there are no colours to see.

92580.q: Why are light-coloured clothes safer on a bike at night?
a: They reflect more light from headlights
92580.e: Light colours reflect a lot of the light from car headlights. That way the cyclist is seen sooner.
92580.m: Light-coloured clothes are easier to see at night.

92581.q: Why do colourful curtains at a sunny window fade over time?
92581.e: Above all the invisible UV light of the sun breaks down dyes little by little. That is why the colours become pale.

92582.q: What do glow-in-the-dark stars on the bedroom ceiling do when you switch off the light?
a: They keep glowing for a while
92582.e: Glow-in-the-dark paint stores some of the light. In the dark it slowly gives it off again as a faint, often greenish glow.
92582.m: Glow-in-the-dark paint keeps glowing for a while in the dark.

92583.q: Which colour comes right next to red in the rainbow?
92583.e: The colours in the rainbow are always in the same order. Orange comes straight after red.
92583.m: In the rainbow, orange follows red.

92584.q: At what time of day are you most likely to see a rainbow?
92584.e: A rainbow only appears when the sun is low. If the sun is too high, the bow lies below the horizon.
92584.m: Rainbows are usually seen in the morning or evening.

92585.q: What happens if you try to walk to the end of a rainbow?
a: It gets bigger and stays still
92585.e: A rainbow is not a thing in a fixed place. It depends on where you are standing and moves with you.
92585.m: You can never reach a rainbow.

92586.q: What shape would a rainbow have if the ground weren't in the way?
92586.e: From the ground you only see part of the circle. From an aeroplane you can sometimes see the whole circle.
92586.m: A rainbow is really a circle.

92587.q: Can you see a rainbow at night too?
92587.e: With a bright full moon and rain, a moonbow can appear. It is faint and usually looks whitish.
92587.m: Rarely there is a moonbow too.

92588.q: What material is a prism for light experiments usually made of?
92588.e: A prism has to be transparent so that light can pass through it. That is why it is usually made of glass or clear plastic.
92588.m: A prism is made of transparent glass.

92589.q: Which colour is bent the least by a prism?
92589.e: Each colour is bent by a different amount in the glass. Red is bent the least.
92589.m: Red light is bent the least in a prism.

92590.q: What happens if you bring the coloured light from a prism back together?
92590.e: With a lens or a second prism you can combine the colours again. Then white light appears again.
92590.m: All the colours together make white light again.

92591.q: What happens to red laser light in a prism?
a: It stays red and is only bent
92591.e: Red laser light has only one colour. The prism can bend it, but it can't split it into more colours.
92591.m: Light of one colour stays one colour in a prism.

92592.q: What happens to the direction of a beam of light in a prism?
a: It turns round in a circle
92592.e: Light is bent when it goes into the glass and out again at an angle. This bending is called refraction.

92593.q: What at a window can throw colourful spots of light onto the wall?
92593.e: A cut crystal has many slanted faces. It works like a prism and splits the sunlight.
92593.m: Glass crystals at the window make colourful spots of light.

92594.q: Which gemstone sparkles in many colours because it splits light like a prism?
92594.e: A cut diamond bends light very strongly. That is why colourful flashes appear in it.
92594.m: Diamonds sparkle in colours because they split light.

92595.q: Apart from a prism, what can split sunlight into colours?
92595.e: Water bends light in a similar way to glass. If a full glass of water stands in the sun, you sometimes see colourful stripes.
92595.m: Water can also split light into colours.

92596.q: Which three colours are often called the primary colours in art lessons?
92596.e: You can mix many other colours from these three paints. This grouping is often taught in art lessons.
92596.m: Red, yellow and blue are the primary colours in the paint box.

92597.q: From which three colours of light does a screen make all its colours?
92597.e: A screen has tiny dots of light in three colours. Depending on how brightly they shine, we see different colours.
92597.m: Screens mix all colours from red, green and blue.

92598.q: Apart from black, which colour cartridges does a colour printer have?
92598.e: Printers mix colours from cyan (blue-green), magenta (pinkish red) and yellow. Black is added for dark areas.
92598.m: A colour printer prints with cyan, magenta and yellow.

92599.q: Can you mix a primary colour from other colours?
92599.e: Primary colours are the starting colours. You need them to mix other colours, not the other way round.

92600.q: Which of these colours is not a primary colour in the paint box?
92600.e: In the paint box, green is not one of the three primary colours. You can make it yourself.
92600.m: Green is not a primary colour in the paint box.

92601.q: What are colours that you mix from two primary colours called?
92601.e: Orange, green and violet are each made from two primary colours. That is why they are called secondary colours.
92601.m: Two primary colours make a secondary colour.

92602.q: What is the smallest number of primary colours you need to mix very many colours with paint?
92602.e: With three suitable primary colours you can mix almost all bright colours. With only two, many shades are missing.
92602.m: Three primary colours are enough for very many mixed colours.

92603.q: Which colour do you get if you mix yellow and blue paint?
92603.e: When painting, yellow and blue make green. With more yellow, the green gets lighter.

92604.q: Which colour do you get from red and yellow paint?
92604.e: Red and yellow together make orange. That is the colour of an orange or a carrot.

92605.q: Which colour do you get from red and blue paint?
92605.e: If you mix red and blue, you get violet. With more blue it gets darker.

92606.q: Which colour do you get if you mix red with lots of white?
92606.e: White makes a colour lighter. So red becomes a light pink.

92607.q: What do you get if you mix black and white paint?
92607.e: Black and white make grey. The more black, the darker it gets.

92608.q: What do you usually get if you mix lots of paints together?
92608.e: Each paint swallows part of the light. If you mix many, almost everything is swallowed and the colour becomes dark.
92608.m: Lots of paints together become dark.

92609.q: Which colour do you get when red and green light fall on the same spot?
92609.e: Light mixes differently from paint. To our eyes, red and green light together look yellow.
92609.m: Red and green light make yellow.

92610.q: Which colour do you get when red and blue light shine together?
92610.e: Red and blue light make a strong pink. This colour is called magenta.
92610.m: Red and blue light make magenta.

92611.q: Which colour can't you mix with paints?
92611.e: When you mix paints, they always swallow more light. That is why you can't mix white; you need it as a colour of its own.
92611.m: You can't mix white from paints.

92612.q: What is the invisible light that comes after violet called?
92612.e: Ultraviolet means “beyond violet”. Our eyes can't see this light, but it can cause sunburn.

92613.q: What is the invisible light beyond red that we feel as warmth called?
92613.e: Infrared means “below red”. We feel it, for example, as the warmth of a stove.

92614.q: What colour is a white sheet of paper when only red light falls on it?
92614.e: White paper reflects any light that falls on it. If only red light reaches it, it looks red.
92614.m: White paper shows the colour of the light.

92615.q: Which light looks more yellowish than white?
92615.e: A candle flame gives off more red and yellow light than blue. That is why its light looks warm and yellowish.

92616.q: What does a white T-shirt often look like under black light?
92616.e: Many washing powders contain brighteners. These turn the lamp's invisible light into visible bluish light.
92616.m: Under black light, white clothes glow bluish.

92617.q: What colour is the Sun when you see it from space?
92617.e: In space there is no air to scatter parts of the light. That is why the Sun looks white there.
92617.m: From space the Sun looks white.

92618.q: What do you get when a red, a green and a blue lamp shine on the same spot?
92618.e: To our eyes, the three colours of light together make white.
92618.m: Red, green and blue light together make white.

92619.q: What is the band of all colours that white light can be split into called?
92619.e: The spectrum goes from red to violet. A rainbow shows it in the sky.
92619.m: White light can be split into a spectrum.

92620.e: On the colour wheel, the colours go round in order. That way you can see which colours are related.
92620.m: On the colour wheel, the colours go round in a circle.

92621.q: Which colour is opposite red on the colour wheel?
92621.e: Opposite colours are very different. The opposite colour of red is green.
92621.m: Red and green are opposite each other on the colour wheel.

92622.q: Which colour is opposite blue on the colour wheel?
92622.e: Blue and orange make a strong pair of colours. Next to each other they look especially bright.
92622.m: Blue and orange are opposite each other on the colour wheel.

92623.q: What are colours that are opposite each other on the colour wheel called?
92623.e: Complementary means “completing”. These colours complete each other and make a strong contrast.
92623.m: Opposite colours are called complementary colours.

92624.q: Which Swiss artist drew a famous colour wheel with twelve colours?
92624.e: This painter and teacher from Bern worked at the Bauhaus. His twelve-part colour wheel is still used in schools today.
92624.m: Johannes Itten designed a famous colour wheel.

92625.q: Which famous German poet studied a colour wheel?
92625.e: The poet wrote a thick book about colours, the “Theory of Colours”. In it he also drew a colour wheel.
92625.m: Goethe wrote a Theory of Colours.

92626.q: Which colours are called warm colours?
92626.e: These colours remind us of fire and the sun. That is why they look warm.
92626.m: Red, orange and yellow are warm colours.

92627.q: What sometimes shimmers in bright colours on a puddle in the road?
92627.e: A wafer-thin layer of oil floats on the water. Light is reflected from its top and bottom and creates colours.
92627.m: A thin film of oil shimmers in rainbow colours.

92628.q: Which bird has large, shimmering tail feathers with eye patterns?
92628.e: The male peacock spreads out a fan of splendid feathers. Depending on the angle, they shimmer green, blue and gold.

92629.q: Why does the underside of a CD shine in bright colours?
a: It gives off its own light
92629.e: On a CD, tiny grooves run close together. They bend the light and split it into colours.
92629.m: Fine grooves make a CD shimmer in colours.

92630.q: What shimmers on the inside of some seashells?
92630.e: Mother-of-pearl is made of many wafer-thin layers. They make the light shimmer in colours.

92631.q: Where does the brilliant blue of some butterfly wings come from?
a: From tiny structures on the scales
92631.e: On the wing scales there are tiny ridges. They mainly reflect blue light, without any blue pigment.
92631.m: Some blue comes from tiny structures, not from pigment.

92632.q: What happens to shimmering colours when you change the angle you look from?
92632.e: Shimmering colours depend on how the light reaches your eyes. If you turn your head, they change.
92632.m: Shimmering colours change with the angle you look from.

92633.q: Which beetle often shimmers metallic green?
92633.e: The shell of the rose chafer shines green like metal. Depending on the light, it also shimmers gold or copper.

92634.q: Which colourful bird by Swiss streams has shimmering blue feathers?
92634.e: The kingfisher's blue comes from fine structures in its feathers. That is why it shines differently depending on the light.
92634.m: The kingfisher has shimmering blue feathers.

92635.q: Why does the sky often glow red in the evening?
a: The light has a long way to travel through the air
The sun gets hotter in the evening
92635.e: When the sun is low, its light has to pass through a lot of air. The blue light is scattered away, and red and orange are left.
92635.m: In the evening the sky is red because the light has a long way to travel.

92636.q: What colour is the sun often when it sets?
92636.e: Just above the horizon, much of the blue part of sunlight is missing. That is why the sun looks orange-red.
92636.m: The setting sun is often orange-red.

92637.q: What is the red glow of mountain peaks at sunset called?
92637.e: The high peaks are still lit by the reddish light of the sun while the valley is already dark. You often see this in Switzerland.
92637.m: Mountains glowing red is called alpenglow.

92638.q: What often makes a red evening sky especially strong?
a: Lots of snow on the ground
92638.e: Tiny dust particles scatter the light even more. After volcanic eruptions or with Saharan dust, the evening sky is often especially colourful.
92638.m: Dust in the air makes the red evening sky stronger.

92639.q: In which direction do you see the red evening sky?
92639.e: The sun sets in the west. That is where the sky glows red in the evening.
92639.m: You see the red evening sky in the west.

92640.q: Why isn't the sun red at midday?
a: Its light has a short way through the air
The clouds are gone at midday
The moon is in front of it
92640.e: At midday the sun is high and its light only passes through a little air. So almost all the colours are kept.
92640.m: At midday, sunlight only travels a short way through the air.

92641.q: What colour is a sunset on Mars?
92641.e: The fine dust on Mars scatters light differently from our air. Photos from Mars rovers show bluish sunsets.

92642.q: What colour is the sky on the Moon?
92642.e: The Moon has no layer of air to scatter light. That is why the sky there is black, even during the day.
92642.m: On the Moon, the sky is black.

92643.q: How does the blue of the sky change high up in the mountains?
92643.e: High up there is less air above us. So less light is scattered and the sky looks dark blue.
92643.m: In the mountains, the sky is a darker blue.

92644.q: Why doesn't the air in a glass look blue?
a: There is far too little air
It is too warm in the glass
92644.e: The blue of the sky only comes from many kilometres of air. A glass full of air is not enough.
92644.m: Only a huge amount of air looks blue.

a: The water droplets scatter all colours equally
They are made of cotton wool
92645.e: The droplets in clouds are much bigger than the particles of air. They scatter all colours about equally, and that makes white.
92645.m: Clouds are white because they scatter all colours.

92646.q: Why do thunderclouds look dark grey?
a: They are so thick that little light gets through
92646.e: Thunderclouds are often many kilometres high. The light is scattered so many times inside them that little reaches the bottom.
92646.m: Thick clouds let little light through.

92647.q: Why does deep water in the sea or a lake look blue?
92647.e: Water swallows red light a little more strongly than blue light. So in deep water, mainly blue is left.
92647.m: Deep water looks blue because it swallows red.

92648.q: Why do faraway mountains often look bluish?
a: Because of all the air in between
Because they are made of blue stone
Because it is always night there
92648.e: There is a lot of air between us and the mountains. It scatters blue light into our eyes and gives the view a bluish tint.
92648.m: Distant mountains look bluish because of the air.

92649.q: What colour is the sky on Mars during the day?
92649.e: Fine reddish dust floats in the thin air of Mars. It colours the daytime sky yellowish to reddish brown.
92649.m: The daytime sky on Mars is reddish brown.

92650.q: What is visibility often like in Switzerland when the Föhn wind blows?
a: Very clear, you can see far
92650.e: The Föhn is a dry, warm wind that blows down from the mountains. The dry air is very clear, the mountains look close and the sky is deep blue.
92650.m: When the Föhn blows, you can often see very far.

92651.q: What does a red colour filter do with white light?
a: It only lets red light through
It only lets blue light through
92651.e: A filter swallows some of the colours. A red filter lets almost only red through.
92651.m: A red filter only lets red through.

92652.q: What does a red colour filter do with the other colours?
92652.e: The other colours are swallowed in the filter. Only red gets through.
92652.m: A colour filter swallows the other colours.

92653.q: Why does red writing on white paper disappear behind red film?
a: The writing and the paper look the same red
The film wipes the writing away
92653.e: Through the red film, only red light comes from the white paper. The red writing looks exactly the same and no longer stands out.
92653.m: Behind red film, red writing disappears.

92654.q: What does a green leaf look like through a red filter?
92654.e: The leaf mainly reflects green light. The red filter doesn't let green through, so the leaf looks dark.
92654.m: Green things look dark through a red filter.

92655.q: What happens if you hold a red and a green filter one behind the other?
92655.e: The first filter only lets red through. The second doesn't let red through, so hardly any light is left.
92655.m: Two different colour filters one behind the other let almost no light through.

92656.q: What do colourful church windows do with sunlight?
92656.e: The coloured glass works like a filter. That is why colourful patches of light fall on the floor inside the church.

92657.q: How did old traffic lights with a white bulb get their red light?
a: Through a red glass in front
Through red paint on the road
92657.e: In front of the bright lamp there was a coloured glass. It only let the red light through.
92657.m: Old traffic lights coloured their light with coloured glass.

92658.q: What does a yellow banana look like through blue film?
92658.e: The blue film lets almost only blue light through. But the banana hardly reflects any blue, so it looks dark.
92658.m: Through blue film, yellow things look dark.

92659.q: What does the world look like through glasses with yellow lenses?
92659.e: The yellow lenses swallow part of the blue light. That is why everything looks tinted yellow.
92659.m: Through yellow lenses, everything looks yellowish.

92660.q: What colours are the lenses of simple cardboard 3D glasses often?
92660.e: One lens is red, the other blue or blue-green. That way each eye only sees part of the picture.
92660.m: Simple 3D glasses have one red and one blue lens.

92661.q: Why do you see a picture in 3D with red and cyan 3D glasses?
a: Each eye sees a slightly different picture
92661.e: Two slightly shifted views are printed in the picture in two colours. Each lens only lets one view through, and the brain puts them together into a 3D picture.
92661.m: Two different pictures for the two eyes make a 3D picture.

92662.q: What do you often notice when you take off red glasses after a long time?
a: Everything looks greenish for a moment
Everything looks red for a moment
92662.e: The eye gets used to the red light and becomes less sensitive to red. After you take them off, the world briefly looks like the opposite colour.
92662.m: After red glasses, the world looks greenish for a moment.

92663.q: Why do skiers often wear goggles with yellow or orange lenses in fog?
a: You can see bumps in the snow better
92663.e: Yellow and orange lenses block a lot of scattered blue light. That makes bumps in the snow clearer.
92663.m: Yellow ski goggles help in fog.

92664.q: What does a blue sky look like through glasses with red lenses?
92664.e: Red lenses let hardly any blue light through. That is why the blue sky looks dark.
92664.m: Through red lenses, blue things look dark.

92665.q: Can special colour-filter glasses help people with red-green colour blindness?
a: Yes, some colours become easier to tell apart
Yes, they cure the eyes for ever
No, they are just for fun
92665.e: Glasses like these filter out certain parts of the light. This makes red and green stand out from each other better, but the colour blindness is not cured.
92665.m: Special glasses help some people tell colours apart better.

92666.q: Why do the colours of a film look strange through red and cyan 3D glasses?
a: Each eye only gets some of the colours
92666.e: The red lens only lets red through, the other only blue-green. The brain has to put together the colours from both eyes, and it doesn't do this perfectly.

92767.q: How does the ground move when an S-wave passes through?
a: Across the direction the wave travels
Only back and forth in the direction it travels
Not at all, it only travels through air
Only in circles at the surface
92767.e: S-waves are shear waves. The particles vibrate at right angles to the direction in which the wave travels, a bit like a rope being shaken.
92767.m: With S-waves, the ground moves across the direction of travel.

92768.q: Which earthquake waves usually cause the most damage to buildings?
92768.e: Surface waves travel along the Earth's surface and have large movements. They arrive last, but they shake buildings the most.
92768.m: Surface waves cause most of the damage in earthquakes.

92769.q: How do some surface waves move the ground during an earthquake?
a: They make it roll up and down like waves in the sea
They lift it by a metre for ever
92769.e: With some surface waves, the particles of ground move in an ellipse. The ground rises and falls like the sea.
92769.m: Some earthquake waves make the ground roll up and down.

92770.q: How do Love waves shake the ground during an earthquake?
a: In a circle around the Earth's core
92770.e: Love waves are surface waves. They move the ground horizontally back and forth, across the direction of travel.
92770.m: Love waves shake the ground sideways back and forth.

92771.q: A P-wave travels through the Earth's crust at 6 km/s. How long does it take to travel 120 km?
92771.e: Time equals distance divided by speed. 120 km ÷ 6 km/s = 20 s.
92771.m: The travel time of a wave is the distance divided by the speed.

92772.q: Why do you sometimes hear a dull rumble during an earthquake?
a: Some of the ground waves pass into the air as sound
The Earth cracks open with a bang
The quake makes the wind stronger
The measuring instruments make the noise
92772.e: If the ground vibrates fast enough, it passes the movement on to the air. The first waves in particular can then be heard as a rumble or thunder.
92772.m: Earthquake waves can be heard as a rumble.

92773.q: How can earthquake waves be used to study the structure of the Earth's interior?
a: How they bend and how fast they travel reveal the layers of rock
They are used to drill holes down to the Earth's core
They bring rock samples to the surface
They colour the layers in the ground
92773.e: Earthquake waves are bent and reflected at the boundaries between layers and change speed depending on the material. From their arrival times at many stations, scientists build a picture of the Earth's interior.
92773.m: Earthquake waves look inside the Earth like X-rays look inside the body.

92774.q: What is the huge water wave called that a strong quake under the seabed can trigger?
92774.e: If the seabed suddenly rises or sinks, the whole column of water above it is moved. The wave can travel thousands of kilometres.
92774.m: An undersea earthquake can trigger a tsunami.

92775.q: Why do you often feel a jolt first and only then stronger shaking during a nearby quake?
a: The faster waves arrive before the slower ones
A quake always consists of two earthquakes
The ground has to warm up first
The air slows down the first waves
92775.e: Different earthquake waves travel at different speeds. The further away the source is, the bigger the time gap between them.
92775.m: Earthquake waves arrive one after another depending on their speed.

92776.q: What does the magnitude of an earthquake describe?
a: The strength of the quake at its source
The damage at a particular place
The length of the quake in minutes
92776.e: The magnitude is a measure of the energy released. It is calculated from measurements by seismometers.
92776.m: The magnitude measures the strength of an earthquake at its source.

92777.q: How is the intensity of an earthquake different from its magnitude?
a: It describes the effects at a particular place
It measures the depth of the source
It gives the time of the quake
It is always exactly twice as big
92777.e: A quake has only one magnitude, but a different intensity at every place. The intensity depends on what people feel and what gets damaged.
92777.m: The intensity describes how strongly a quake is felt at a place.

92778.q: Which instrument is used to measure earthquake waves?
92778.e: A seismometer records the tiniest movements of the ground. The location and magnitude of a quake are calculated from the measurements.

92779.q: Which scale for the strength of earthquakes is often mentioned in the news?
92779.e: The Richter scale was developed by Charles Richter in 1935. Today experts use similar scales, but the news often still talks about the Richter scale.
92779.m: The strength of earthquakes is often given on the Richter scale.

92780.q: Can the magnitude of an earthquake be negative?
a: Only for quakes under the sea
92780.e: The magnitude scale has no lower limit. Sensitive seismometers also measure tiny quakes with values below zero.
92780.m: Very small earthquakes can have a negative magnitude.

92781.q: With each step of magnitude, the energy increases about 32 times. How many times more energy does a magnitude 6 quake release than a magnitude 4 quake?
92781.e: Two steps mean 32 × 32 = 1024. That is about 1000 times more energy.
92781.m: Two steps of magnitude mean about a thousand times more energy.

92782.q: From what magnitude does an earthquake usually cause major damage in populated areas?
92782.e: You can hardly feel quakes below 3. From a magnitude of about 6, buildings often collapse, especially if they are not built to withstand earthquakes.
92782.m: Earthquakes of magnitude 6 and above are usually destructive.

92783.q: Who developed the best-known scale for measuring the strength of earthquakes in 1935?
92783.e: The American seismologist Charles Francis Richter presented his scale in 1935. It still bears his name today.
92783.m: Charles Francis Richter developed the Richter scale in 1935.

92785.q: What does an earthquake of magnitude 2 on the Richter scale mean for people?
a: You hardly feel it or not at all
92785.e: Quakes of magnitude 2 are very weak. They are recorded by instruments but usually not noticed by people.
92785.m: You can hardly feel earthquakes with a small magnitude.

92786.q: Roughly what magnitude does an earthquake have that can cause major damage?
92786.e: Quakes from magnitude 6 to 7 can badly damage houses. You can hardly feel quakes of around magnitude 1 or 2.
92786.m: Strong earthquakes have a magnitude of about 7.

92787.q: One quake has a Richter magnitude of 5, another of 2. How many times bigger is the swing on the seismogram for the stronger one?
92787.e: Each step means a swing ten times bigger, and the difference is three steps. 10 × 10 × 10 = 1000.
92787.m: Three steps on the Richter scale mean a swing a thousand times bigger.

92788.q: Does the Richter scale have a fixed maximum value?
a: No, it has no upper limit
92788.e: The scale has no upper limit. But in nature, quakes far above magnitude 9.5 are hardly possible, because ruptures in rock cannot get endlessly big.
92788.m: The Richter scale has no upper limit.

92789.q: How much bigger is the swing on the seismogram at magnitude 6 than at magnitude 5?
92789.e: The Richter scale is built so that each step means a swing ten times bigger. So from 5 to 6 it is ten times as much.
92789.m: One step more on the Richter scale means a swing ten times bigger.

92790.e: A seismometer measures the movements of the ground. The strength of a quake is calculated from its recordings.

92791.q: On what principle does a classic seismometer work?
a: A heavy mass stays still while the ground moves
A thermometer measures the heat of the quake
A microphone listens to the rumbling in the ground
92791.e: The heavy mass hangs loosely in the casing. Because of its inertia it stays almost still, and the movement of the casing relative to the mass is measured.
92791.m: A seismometer uses the inertia of a mass.

92792.q: To which planet did the InSight probe take a seismometer in 2018 that ETH Zurich had helped to build?
92792.e: The InSight probe landed on Mars in November 2018. Its seismometer recorded more than 1300 marsquakes.
92792.m: There are quakes on Mars too.

92793.q: What did the seismometers set up on the Moon by Apollo astronauts detect?
a: A magnetic field like the Earth's
92793.e: The instruments recorded vibrations from 1969 to 1977. These included moonquakes and meteorite impacts.
92793.m: There are moonquakes on the Moon.

92794.q: Why are seismometers often placed in tunnels, caves or boreholes?
a: There, traffic and wind disturb the measurements less
They are closer to the Earth's core there
92794.e: Seismometers are very sensitive and also register lorries or gusts of wind. Underground they are better shielded from such disturbances.
92794.m: Underground, seismometers measure with less disturbance.

92795.q: What is the minimum number of measuring stations needed to find the epicentre of a quake from the distances?
92795.e: Each station only knows its distance to the quake, so a circle around itself. Only three circles cross at a single point.
92795.m: With three stations you can locate an epicentre.

92796.q: In which three directions does a modern seismometer measure ground movement?
a: Forwards, backwards and in a circle
To the north, to the Earth's core and to the sun
92796.e: Ground movement is three-dimensional. That is why a modern seismometer measures in three directions, one vertical and two horizontal.
92796.m: Modern seismometers measure in three directions.

92797.q: What is the curve recorded by a seismometer during an earthquake called?
92797.e: The seismometer records the ground movement as a zigzag line. This recording is called a seismogram. The stronger the quake, the bigger the swings.
92797.m: A seismogram shows the ground movement during a quake.

92798.q: What does a modern seismometer turn ground movement into?
92798.e: In the past, needles scratched the curves on paper. Today coils and sensors produce electrical signals that are stored and sent digitally.
92798.m: Modern seismometers deliver their measurements as electrical signals.

92799.q: What is the hypocentre of an earthquake?
a: The place inside the Earth where the rupture begins
The point with the most damage
The measuring station that notices the quake first
The highest point of the quake zone
92799.e: At the hypocentre, the rock begins to break. From there, earthquake waves spread out in all directions.
92799.m: The hypocentre is the source of an earthquake inside the Earth.

92800.q: Which term means the same as hypocentre?
92800.e: Hypocentre and focus are two names for the same place. “Hypo” is Greek and means “under”.
92800.m: Focus is another word for hypocentre.

92801.q: A source is 30 km deep, and a station is 40 km from the epicentre. How far is the station from the hypocentre?
92801.e: Depth and distance form a right-angled triangle. By Pythagoras, 30² + 40² = 900 + 1600 = 2500, and its square root is 50.
92801.m: You calculate the distance to the source with Pythagoras' theorem.

92802.q: What is the point on the Earth's surface directly above the hypocentre called?
92802.e: The hypocentre is inside the Earth. The point directly above it on the surface is called the epicentre, and the quake is often felt most strongly there.
92802.m: The epicentre is on the surface above the source of the quake.

92803.q: In which directions do earthquake waves spread from the hypocentre?
92803.e: From the source, the waves travel through the rock in all directions, like when you drop a stone into water. This is how they reach measuring stations all over the world.
92803.m: Earthquake waves spread from the source in all directions.

92804.q: Where do deep earthquakes mainly occur?
a: In subduction zones, where one plate sinks under another
92804.e: The sinking plate is colder and more brittle than the surrounding mantle. That is why ruptures can still happen in it at great depth.
92804.m: Deep earthquakes happen where tectonic plates sink down.

92805.q: Why does a shallow quake often cause more damage than an equally strong deep one?
a: The waves have a shorter path and lose less energy
Shallow quakes always last for days
Deep quakes never reach the surface
92805.e: Earthquake waves get weaker on their way through the rock. So with a nearby source, more energy arrives at the surface.
92805.m: Shallow earthquakes are often especially destructive at the surface.

92806.q: At what depth are the sources of most earthquakes in Switzerland?
92806.e: Swiss earthquakes happen in the Earth's crust. In the Alps, the sources are often even less than 15 km deep.
92806.m: Earthquakes in Switzerland mostly have shallow sources in the Earth's crust.

92807.q: What destroyed large parts of the city of Basel in 1356?
92807.e: On 18 October 1356, a strong earthquake shook the city of Basel. Afterwards, a big fire also broke out in the city.
92807.m: In 1356, an earthquake destroyed large parts of Basel.

92808.q: What destroyed a large part of the city's wooden houses after the Basel earthquake of 1356?
a: A fire in the city that lasted for days
92808.e: Overturned cooking fires and lamps set the city on fire. According to the sources, the fire raged for eight days.
92808.m: After the Basel earthquake, the city burned for days.

92809.q: Roughly where was the centre of the Basel earthquake of 1356?
92809.e: According to modern studies, the source of the quake was only a few kilometres south of Basel, near Reinach in Basel-Landschaft.
92809.m: The centre of the Basel earthquake was close to Basel.

92810.q: Which famous building in Basel was badly damaged in the earthquake of 1356?
92810.e: At Basel Minster, the choir collapsed and the roof fell into the nave. The other buildings did not even exist then.
92810.m: In 1356, Basel Minster was badly damaged.

92811.q: What happened to the castles in the wider area during the Basel earthquake?
a: Not a single one was hit
All stayed intact thanks to thick walls
They were all flooded by the Rhine
92811.e: Over a wide area around Basel, about 40 castles were badly hit. Many were rebuilt afterwards, others remained ruins.
92811.m: The Basel earthquake destroyed many castles in the region.

92812.q: Why did probably fewer people die in the Basel earthquake than you might expect?
a: Many had fled the city after a foreshock
The city was uninhabited at the time
All the houses were built to withstand earthquakes
It happened in the middle of the night
92812.e: A foreshock in the afternoon had warned people, and many left the city. Even so, the figures for the number of dead vary widely, between about 100 and 2000.
92812.m: A foreshock saved many people's lives in the Basel earthquake.

92813.q: What place does the Basel earthquake of 1356 hold in the history of Central Europe?
a: It is the strongest historically recorded quake
It is the most recent strong quake
It is the only quake with a tsunami
It is the weakest known quake
92813.e: No other recorded earthquake in Central Europe was as strong. That is why it serves as an important yardstick for the danger in the region.
92813.m: The Basel earthquake is the strongest recorded quake in Central Europe.

92814.q: Roughly what magnitude did the Basel earthquake of 1356 have, according to modern estimates?
92814.e: As there were no measuring instruments in 1356, the magnitude is estimated from the recorded damage. Estimates are between about 6 and 7; 6.6 is often given.
92814.m: According to estimates, the Basel earthquake had a magnitude between 6 and 7.

92815.q: How do we know so much today about the Basel earthquake of 1356, even though there were no measuring instruments?
a: From old reports and damage to buildings
From photos taken at the time
92815.e: Chroniclers wrote down what was destroyed, and on old walls such as at the Lohnhof you can still see damage from the quake today. Experts estimate the strength from this.
92815.m: Old reports and damage to buildings tell us about the Basel earthquake.

92816.q: What is the main task of the Swiss Seismological Service?
92816.e: The Seismological Service records all quakes in Switzerland and provides information about them. Its roots go back to the Earthquake Commission of 1878.
92816.m: The Swiss Seismological Service monitors earthquakes in Switzerland.

92817.q: Roughly how many seismic measuring stations does the Swiss Seismological Service run?
92817.e: The stations are spread across the whole country. Some are in caves, tunnels or boreholes.
92817.m: The Seismological Service monitors Switzerland with over 200 measuring stations.

92818.q: On average, how many earthquakes a year can people feel in Switzerland?
92818.e: Most recorded quakes are too weak to feel. Only 10 to 20 a year on average are noticed by the population.
92818.m: In Switzerland, about 10 to 20 earthquakes are felt each year.

92819.q: How quickly does the Swiss Seismological Service publish the first automatic information about a quake?
92819.e: The measurement data are analysed automatically. The location, time and strength appear on the website within about 90 seconds.
92819.m: The first information about a quake appears after about 90 seconds.

92820.q: Why can earthquake instruments also detect banned nuclear bomb tests?
a: Underground explosions shake the ground like earthquakes
Nuclear bombs send out radio waves
92820.e: Underground nuclear tests cause vibrations like earthquakes. A station near Davos is part of a worldwide network that monitors the ban on such tests.
92820.m: Seismometers also help to detect banned nuclear tests.

92821.q: In which app does the Swiss Seismological Service publish earthquake reports from magnitude 2.5?
92821.e: Quakes from magnitude 2.5 are also shown in the MeteoSwiss app. The service also provides information on its website and on naturgefahren.ch.
92821.m: Earthquake reports from magnitude 2.5 appear in the MeteoSwiss app.

92822.q: Who else does the Swiss Seismological Service inform about large damaging quakes abroad?
92822.e: After big disaster quakes anywhere in the world, help from Switzerland may be needed. That is why the Humanitarian Aid Unit is informed quickly.
92822.m: After big quakes abroad, the Seismological Service informs humanitarian aid.

92823.q: Who monitors earthquakes in Switzerland on behalf of the federal government?
a: The Seismological Service at ETH Zurich
The fire brigade of each municipality
92823.e: Since 1914, monitoring earthquakes has been a federal task. Today the Swiss Seismological Service is a unit of ETH Zurich.
92823.m: The Swiss Seismological Service is part of ETH Zurich.
